takeaways: The ASIC design flow runs specification, architecture, RTL, verification, synthesis, DFT insertion, physical design and signoff to tapeout; fabrication, wafer probe, packaging and final test follow.
Test is designed in: scan chains and BIST are added at the netlist stage, ATPG patterns come from the netlist, and splitting one 5,000-flop chain into ten cuts scan test time about ten times.
ASICs differ in what is made for one design: every mask (full-custom, standard-cell), only metal masks (gate array) or nothing (PLD, FPGA); total cost = NRE + N × unit cost decides by volume.
A Verilog module with its ports is the unit of design; nets are driven continuously, variables hold values between procedural assignments, and widths and x values change what an expression gives.
Gate-level, dataflow and behavioural code can describe the same circuit; only the synthesizable subset becomes hardware, and a combinational always block must assign every output on every path.
A test bench has no ports: it drives the DUT, waits, compares with expected values and reports PASS or FAIL, so errors are caught in simulation instead of in silicon.
An FPGA is an array of LUTs, flip-flops, routing and I/O blocks set by configuration memory; ROMs, PALs and PLAs implement the same logic with fixed or programmable AND and OR planes.
Floorplanning, placement and routing decide wire length, congestion, timing and power; utilization and HPWL put numbers on a floorplan and a placement.

IP cores (soft, firm or hard) and soft-core processors let an SoC reuse verified blocks, with wrappers, an aligned memory map without overlaps, clock-domain crossing and a test wrapper for buried cores.
bank_note: Most syllabi build long answers round the ASIC design flow with its artifacts, the three Verilog modelling styles shown with short code, test benches, FPGA architecture and the economics of ASIC styles, so draw the figure first, then label each stage with its input, output and check.

svg.aria: The ASIC design flow in three rows: front end from specification to synthesis, back end from DFT insertion to tapeout, and the foundry steps after tapeout, with a verification band beside the flow.

answer: A design flow is the ordered set of stages that turns a specification into a chip. Each stage refines the description, hands a checked file to the next, and keeps the problem small enough to check.

answer.text: Stage by stage, with what goes in, what comes out and what is checked:

head: Stage
Input
Artifact produced
Check before moving on
rows: Spec document: function, MHz, mW, pins, cost
Block diagram, clock and power domains, memory sizes, bus widths
Every feature tested; coverage target met
Scan netlist, BIST blocks, test patterns
Core size, macro and pin positions, power grid
DRC, LVS, static timing, power, IR drop

answer: Front end: specification, architecture, RTL, verification and synthesis. It ends with the gate netlist. The work is in text and netlists, and a bug costs an edit and a re-run.
Back end: DFT insertion, floorplanning, placement, clock-tree synthesis, routing and signoff. It ends with the GDSII layout. The work is geometry on the die, and a bug costs a re-layout.

Verification is not one box. RTL simulation starts it; after synthesis, equivalence checking proves the netlist matches the RTL; after routing, static timing analysis and gate-level simulation check the real wire delays.

Test is designed in. Scan chains and BIST go in at the netlist stage so that physical design places and times them like any other logic; ATPG then produces the patterns that the tester applies after fabrication.
After tapeout the foundry makes the masks and wafers; wafer probe marks bad dies, good dies are diced and packaged, and final test on ATE screens each chip before it ships.

Closing check with numbers: for a 24-lakh-gate SoC that synthesises at 1,20,000 gates/h (20 h), places and routes at 60,000 gates/h (40 h) and needs 3 h of verification per 10,000 gates (720 h), verification is 720 ÷ 780 = 92.3 % of the flow time. That is why verification is drawn as a track beside the whole flow, not as one step.

bank.q: Classify Verilog operators into arithmetic, bitwise, reduction, logical, relational, shift, conditional and concatenation, and give a one-line example of each.
outline: Arithmetic: +, -, *, /, % on vectors, sized results
Bitwise: &, |, ^, ~ operate bit by bit on equal-width operands
Reduction: unary &, |, ^ fold all bits of one operand into a single bit
Logical: &&, ||, ! treat a nonzero vector as true and return 1 bit
Relational and equality: <, >, <=, >=, ==, != (and ===, !==) return 1 bit
Shift: <<, >> fill with zeros; >>> copies the sign bit of a signed operand
Conditional: cond ? a : b is a two-way select
Concatenation and replication: {a,b} and {n{a}}
answer: Take two 4-bit unsigned values for every example: p = 4'b1011 (11) and q = 4'b0101 (5). Every result below was printed by a simulator run.

answer.text: The operator classes, with one example each:

head: Class
Operators
Example
Result
rows: p + q into a 5-bit target; p − q; p * q into 8 bits; p / q; p % q
p & q; p | q; p ^ q; ~p

answer: Arithmetic operators work on the whole vector. The width of the result is set by the widest operand and by the target: p + q = 16 needs 5 bits, so a 4-bit target keeps only 0000 and loses the carry. Integer division truncates toward zero and % takes the sign of the first operand.

Bitwise operators work bit by bit and give a vector as wide as the operands: 1011 & 0101 = 0001. Reduction operators take one operand and fold all its bits into one bit: &1011 = 1 & 0 & 1 & 1 = 0, and ^0101 = 0 because q has an even number of 1s (this is the parity bit).
Logical operators treat any nonzero value as true and return one bit: p && q = 1 because both are nonzero, and !p = 0. Do not confuse !p (one bit, 0) with ~p (four bits, 0100).
Relational and equality operators return one bit. == and != give x if any compared bit is x or z; === and !== compare x and z as values, so they are used in test benches to catch an x output.
Logical shifts fill with zeros: 1011 >> 2 = 0010. The arithmetic right shift >>> copies the sign bit only when the operand is signed: $signed(1011) is −5 and −5 >>> 2 = 1110, which is −2.

The conditional operator is a 2-to-1 multiplexer: cond ? a : b gives a when cond is true. Concatenation joins bits ({p[1:0], q} = 11 followed by 0101 = 110101 = 53), and replication repeats them ({2{q}} = 01010101; {{2{p[3]}}, p} = 111011 sign-extends p to 6 bits).

Precedence, high to low: unary operators and reductions, **, * / %, + −, shifts, relational, equality, bitwise &, ^, |, logical &&, ||, and ?: lowest. So a + b * c > d ? x : y groups as ((a + (b * c)) > d) ? x : y.

Closing check: with a = 4, b = 3, c = 2, d = 1 (4-bit), a + b * c = 10 > 1 is true, so a + b * c > d ? (a << 1) : ~b gives a << 1 = 8 = 1000, the result of the parse-tree figure in the Verilog chapter.

outline: Gate level: primitive instances (and, or, not) or instantiated cells; closest to the netlist
Dataflow: continuous assign with operators; shows data movement
Behavioural: always block with if/else or case; algorithmic, needs synthesis rules
Code for each style of the same mux
Which style is used for structural netlists, which for arithmetic, which for control logic and FSMs
answer: The three levels describe the same hardware at different distances from the netlist. The specification here: y = a when sel = 0 and y = b when sel = 1, that is y = sel′·a + sel·b.

answer.text: Gate-level (structural) model. Primitive gates are instanced by name, output first; internal nets are wires:
Dataflow model. One continuous assignment drives the output whenever an input changes:
Behavioural model. An always block with a full sensitivity list and an if with an else, so no latch is inferred; y is declared reg because it is assigned in a procedural block:

head: Point

answer: Switch-level modelling sits below gate level: nmos, pmos and cmos primitives model transistors as switches. A CMOS inverter is one pmos from vdd to y and one nmos from y to gnd, both gated by a. It is used for MOS circuit and cell simulation, not for synthesis.

Real RTL mixes the levels: assign statements for datapath equations, always @(posedge clk) blocks with nonblocking <= for registers, and module instances to join blocks. Synthesis turns all three into the same kind of gate netlist.

bank.q: Describe the architecture of an FPGA: logic cells, LUTs, flip-flops, routing and I/O blocks. How is the function configured?
outline: Array of configurable logic blocks (CLBs); each CLB holds LUTs, flip-flops and carry logic
A k-input LUT is a 2ᵏ × 1 memory that stores the truth table, so any k-input function fits
Programmable interconnect: switch boxes and connection boxes driven by configuration bits
I/O blocks with selectable standards and registers
Configuration memory loaded as a bitstream at power-up
Trade-off versus ASIC: no mask cost, lower speed and higher area
answer: An FPGA (field-programmable gate array) is a chip of identical logic blocks in a grid, wire segments between them, and I/O blocks round the edge. Every choice (the logic each block does, which wires join, how each pin behaves) is held in configuration memory that the user loads.

Logic block: a configurable logic block (CLB, the Xilinx name; LAB in Intel parts) holds several logic cells. Each cell is a lookup table (LUT), a flip-flop, a bypass multiplexer that picks the LUT output or the registered output, and fast carry logic for adders.
LUT: an n-input LUT is a 2ⁿ × 1 memory whose n inputs are the address. It stores the truth table, so it implements any function of n inputs. A 4-input LUT holds 2⁴ = 16 bits; a 6-input LUT holds 64.

answer.text: Example: f = A·B + C·D in a 4-input LUT. The 16 stored bits, address ABCD from 0000 to 1111:

answer: For A = 1, B = 1, C = 0, D = 1 the address is 1101 = 13, and the bit stored there is 1, as A·B = 1 requires.

Routing: horizontal and vertical channels of wire segments of several lengths. A connection box joins a block's pins to the channel wires; a switch box at each crossing joins segments. Each switch is a pass transistor or multiplexer controlled by one configuration bit. Routing often takes most of the delay and area of an FPGA.
I/O blocks (IOBs) sit at the pads: input and output buffers with selectable voltage standards, drive strength and slew rate, plus input and output registers.
Hard blocks: block RAM, DSP slices (multiply-accumulate), clock managers (PLLs), and in large parts transceivers and processor cores.

Configuration: synthesis maps the HDL to LUTs and flip-flops, packing groups them into blocks, placement and routing choose sites and switches, and bitstream generation writes every configuration bit. In an SRAM FPGA the bitstream is loaded at each power-up from flash or a host, because SRAM is volatile; flash FPGAs keep it without power, and antifuse FPGAs are programmed once.

Trade-off against an ASIC: no NRE and no mask, a new bitstream fixes a bug, and a board can be ready in hours. The price is a higher unit cost, a lower clock rate and more power and area for the same function, because programmable switches and LUTs replace fixed wires and gates.

Closing check with numbers: 3,000 such functions at 15 % packing loss need 3,000 ÷ 0.85 = 3,529.4, so 3,530 LUTs, and 3,530 × 16 = 56,480 configuration bits for the LUTs alone, before any routing bits.

bank.q: What is design for testability? Explain scan insertion, ATPG and BIST, and where the DUT and tester fit in the flow.
outline: Why testing matters: stuck-at and other faults, defective parts must be screened
Scan: flip-flops replaced by scan flip-flops chained into shift registers, giving controllability and observability
ATPG: excite a fault, propagate to an output, generate compact pattern sets
BIST: on-chip LFSR pattern generator plus signature analyser (MISR)
Flow position: DFT insertion after synthesis, patterns after netlist, DUT tested on ATE with test program
Metrics: fault coverage, pattern count, test time and test cost
answer: Design for testability (DFT) is hardware added during design so that a tester can control and observe the inside of a chip. Manufacturing defects (shorts, opens, bad vias) are certain on some dies, and a tester sees only the pins, so without DFT most internal nodes cannot be tested.

Faults are modelled so that tests can be computed. The stuck-at model treats a line as fixed at 0 or 1; transition and path delay models treat it as too slow; bridging models treat two lines as shorted.

answer.text: A test must excite the fault and make it visible. For a 2-input AND gate y = a·b:

answer: Scan insertion: after synthesis each flip-flop is replaced by a scan flip-flop, a flip-flop with a multiplexer in front. When scan enable is 1 the flip-flops join into a shift register (a scan chain) from a scan-in pin to a scan-out pin. A test shifts a pattern in, pulses one functional clock to capture the logic's response, and shifts the result out while the next pattern shifts in. Every flip-flop becomes directly controllable and observable, so a sequential circuit is tested like a combinational one.

ATPG (automatic test pattern generation) works on the scan netlist and the fault list. For each fault it finds inputs that excite it and a path that carries the error to a scan flip-flop or an output (algorithms such as the D-algorithm and PODEM). Fault simulation then marks every other fault each pattern also detects, so the set stays small. The result is fault coverage = detected faults ÷ total faults.

BIST (built-in self-test) puts the tester on the chip: a linear-feedback shift register (LFSR) makes pseudo-random patterns and a multiple-input signature register (MISR) compresses the responses into a signature compared with the expected one. Example: a 3-bit LFSR that shifts left and feeds Q2 ⊕ Q1 into Q0, seeded 001, runs 001, 010, 101, 011, 111, 110, 100 and back to 001, all 7 nonzero states. BIST is standard for memories and runs at full speed, at the cost of area.
Boundary scan (IEEE 1149.1, JTAG) adds a scan cell at every pin behind the TDI, TDO, TCK and TMS test access port, so the board connections between chips can be tested.

Where they sit in the flow: DFT insertion comes after synthesis and before physical design, so scan chains are placed, routed and timed; ATPG runs on the final netlist; the patterns are written into a tester program. After fabrication each die is the DUT (device under test): it is tested at wafer probe and again after packaging on automatic test equipment (ATE).

Closing check with numbers: 1,000 patterns on one chain of 5,000 flip-flops at 50 MHz take (1,000 × 5,001 + 5,000) × 20 ns = 100.12 ms per chip, ₹0.30 at ₹3 per tester-second; ten chains of 500 take 10.03 ms and ₹0.03. Test cost is a design decision.

bank.q: Write a synthesizable Verilog module for a 4-bit synchronous up counter with asynchronous reset. Add a test bench, and explain how it is compiled and simulated.
outline: Module declaration with ports clk, reset, count[3:0]; count declared reg
always @(posedge clk or posedge reset) with nonblocking assignment count <= count + 1
Test bench with no ports, reg for clock and reset, wire for count, DUT instantiated by name
Clock generation by always #5 clk = ~clk with clk starting at 0; reset pulse then repeated clock edges
Correct use of nonblocking assignment in sequential logic
Compile and elaborate with a simulator, run, inspect waveforms or $monitor output

answer.text: The counter. The reset is asynchronous because posedge reset is in the event list; the count is synchronous because it changes only on posedge clk:

answer: Why it is synthesizable: one clocked always block, an if that tests reset first (the pattern synthesis tools map to a flip-flop with an asynchronous clear), constant widths and no delays. count is declared reg because it is assigned in a procedural block; synthesis builds it as four D flip-flops and a 4-bit incrementer.

Nonblocking <= is used because count is a register: the right side is read at the clock edge and all registers update together at the end of the time step, so no other block can see a half-updated value.
Wrap-around: count is 4 bits, so after 1111 (15) the sum 10000 is cut to 0000 and counting restarts. No extra code is needed.

answer.text: The test bench. It has no ports; clk and reset are reg because the bench drives them, count is a wire because the DUT drives it:

answer: Clock: clk starts at 0 and toggles every 5 ns, so the period is 10 ns and the rising edges come at 5, 15, 25 ns and so on. Without the = 0 start, clk would stay x for ever, because ~x is x.
Reset: reset is 1 from 0 to 12 ns, so the edge at 5 ns keeps count at 0. Reset is released at 12 ns, away from any clock edge, so there is no race.

Compile and run (Icarus Verilog): iverilog -o tc tb_counter4.v counter4.v compiles and elaborates both files with tb_counter4 as the top; vvp tc runs the simulation. $monitor prints a line each time a listed signal changes, and gtkwave counter.vcd shows the waveforms.

answer.text: Expected output (printed by the run):

answer: Closing check: the first edge after reset is at 15 ns, so count reaches 15 after 15 edges, at 15 + 14 × 10 = 155 ns, and wraps to 0 at the next edge, 165 ns, exactly as the run printed. The simulation stops at 12 + 170 = 182 ns.

bank.q: Write Verilog for a 1-bit full adder in gate level and in dataflow style, and write a test bench that applies all input combinations and checks the outputs.
outline: Gate level: two xor, two and, one or primitive instances with named wires
Dataflow: assign sum = a ^ b ^ cin; assign cout = (a & b) | (b & cin) | (a & cin);
Test bench: regs a, b, cin; wires sum, cout; instantiate both versions
Stimulus: exhaustive loop or #10 steps through 8 input combinations
$monitor or $display and a self-check against expected values
Observation: both descriptions must match at every step
answer: A full adder adds a, b and a carry-in cin: sum = a ⊕ b ⊕ cin and cout = a·b + cin·(a ⊕ b), which equals a·b + b·cin + a·cin.

answer.text: Gate level, built as two half adders and an OR. The internal nets s1 = a ⊕ b, c1 = a·b and c2 = s1·cin are declared as wires:
Dataflow, one assign per output:

answer: The two carry forms agree: a·b + s1·cin uses a ⊕ b, the dataflow form uses a + b. They differ only when a = b = 1, and then a·b = 1 already sets the carry.

answer.text: Self-checking test bench. A loop counter i from 0 to 7 is split into the three inputs, so all 8 combinations are applied; the expected two-bit result is simply a + b + cin:

answer: Points in the bench: {a, b, cin} = i assigns the low 3 bits of i to the inputs; #10 lets both adders settle before the compare; !== makes an x output count as an error; the compare width is 2 bits because {c_g, s_g} is 2 bits wide, so a + b + cin is worked out to 2 bits and keeps its carry.

answer.text: The run prints (abc, then cout sum from each model):

answer: and ends with PASS: 8 of 8. To prove the checker works, change g5 to an and gate: rows 011, 101, 110 and 111 need c1 or c2 alone, and the run then reports FAIL: 4.
Closing check: row 111 gives 1 + 1 + 1 = 3 = binary 11, so cout = 1 and sum = 1, matching the last column of both models.

bank.q: A netlist of 1,00,000 standard cells is ready. Explain what floorplanning, placement and routing do to it, in order, and what is checked after each.
outline: Floorplan: die size and aspect ratio, macro and memory positions, I/O pin assignment, power plan, placement blockages
Checks: area utilisation, pin accessibility, power-grid IR drop estimate
Placement: global then detailed, rows of standard cells, objectives of wire length and congestion, timing-driven placement
Checks: congestion map, estimated timing, cell density, no overlaps
Clock-tree synthesis between placement and routing
Routing: global routing assigns regions, detailed routing draws wires and vias; DRC, timing and crosstalk checks after routing
answer: Input: a gate netlist of 1,00,000 standard cells with timing constraints. Output: a routed, signed-off layout (GDSII). Assume an average cell area of 2.5 µm² so the size can be worked out.

answer.text: Floorplanning: size the core. Cell area = 1,00,000 × 2.5 µm² = 2,50,000 µm² = 0.25 mm². At a target utilization of 70 %:
answer.pre:
A<sub>core</sub> = A<sub>used</sub> ÷ U = 0.25 mm² ÷ 0.70 = 0.357 mm²
square core: side = √0.357 = 0.598 mm, about 0.6 mm × 0.6 mm

answer: Floorplanning also places the hard macros (SRAMs, PLLs) near the logic they serve and with their pins facing the core, assigns the I/O pins to the side where their signals go, builds the power grid (VDD and VSS rings and straps) and adds placement blockages round the macros.

Checks after floorplanning: utilization (here 70 %, leaving 30 % for routing, buffers and decoupling cells), aspect ratio near 1 unless the macros need otherwise, pin access, and an early IR-drop estimate of the power grid.

Placement: global placement spreads the 1,00,000 cells to cut total wire length and congestion, ignoring exact sites; legalization and detailed placement then snap each cell into a legal, non-overlapping site in a row. Timing-driven placement pulls the cells of critical paths together.

answer.text: Wire length is estimated by HPWL. Swapping two cells can cut it: with A(1, 1), B(5, 1), C(1, 4), D(5, 4) and nets {A, D}, {B, C}, {A, B, C}:

head: Net
HPWL before
HPWL after swapping A and B

answer: Checks after placement: no overlaps, cell density per region, the congestion map, and timing with estimated wires.

Clock-tree synthesis comes next: buffers are inserted so the clock reaches every flip-flop with small skew and an acceptable insertion delay. It must come before routing because the clock buffers are real cells that must be placed and wired.

Routing: global routing assigns each net to routing regions and checks that no region needs more tracks than it has; detailed routing then picks exact tracks, layers and vias, obeying width and spacing rules.

Checks after routing (signoff): DRC (geometry rules), LVS (layout netlist equals source netlist), static timing with extracted wire resistance and capacitance (setup and hold), crosstalk, power and IR drop, and antenna rules. Only then is the GDSII taped out.
Closing check: 0.598 mm × 0.598 mm = 0.358 mm², and 0.25 ÷ 0.358 = 0.70, so the core meets the 70 % target; the swap cut the placement estimate from 21 to 13 units, 38 %.

bank.q: You must add a soft-core processor to an FPGA system-on-chip. Explain the steps: bus connection, memory map, wrapper and clock-domain crossing.
outline: Select a soft core and its bus interface (a standard on-chip bus such as AXI or AHB)
Check that the core fits every FPGA resource, not only LUTs
Assign address ranges to program memory, data memory and peripherals; document the memory map
Wrap the processor and each peripheral with a wrapper that adapts signals and bus protocol
Reset and interrupt wiring, boot memory contents
Clock-domain crossing: synchronisers for single bits, asynchronous FIFOs for data
Verify with a test bench that runs a small program through the memory map
answer: Choose the core and its bus. A soft core (for example MicroBlaze, Nios V or an open RISC-V core) comes as RTL with a bus interface such as AXI or AHB. Pick the options (cache, multiplier, debug) that the software needs.

answer.text: Check that it fits every resource. For an FPGA with 12,000 LUTs, 20 DSP slices and 30 BRAMs and a core needing 1,800 LUTs, 4 DSP slices and 6 BRAMs:

answer: So at most 5 cores fit; one core uses 15 % of the LUTs, 20 % of the DSP slices and 20 % of the BRAMs, leaving room for the peripherals.
Connect it to the bus: the CPU is the bus master; memories and peripherals are slaves behind an interconnect that decodes the address and routes each transfer.

answer.text: Write the memory map. End address = base + size − 1, each base a multiple of its size, no overlaps:

answer: A DSP block first proposed at 0x2000_8000 would have ended at 0x2000_FFFF, inside the SRAM range; moving it to 0x5000_0000 removes the clash. The firmware header file and the interconnect decoder are both generated from this one table.

Wrap each block: a wrapper adapts the block's own signals to the bus protocol (address, data, valid and ready handshakes), holds its control and status registers, and may add a register slice to meet timing.

Reset, interrupts and boot: state the reset polarity and whether it is synchronous or asynchronous, release the CPU from reset after the clock is stable, wire the peripheral interrupts to the CPU's interrupt controller, and load the boot ROM (or a BRAM) with the first program.

Clock-domain crossing: if the UART runs on its own clock, every signal between the two domains needs a crossing circuit. A single control bit goes through a two-flip-flop synchroniser; a multi-bit value goes through an asynchronous FIFO or a handshake, never through a plain two-flop synchroniser, because its bits could be caught on different cycles.
Verify: run the core's own tests, add bus protocol checks, then simulate the whole SoC with a small program that writes and reads every block at its address and prints through the UART.
Closing check: 16 KB = 0x4000, so 0x0000_0000 + 0x4000 − 1 = 0x0000_3FFF; 32 KB = 0x8000, and 0x5000_0000 ÷ 0x8000 = 0xA000 exactly, so the DSP base is aligned.

bank.q: A start-up in Chennai must ship 5,000 units of a signal-processing board in six months. Compare an ASIC and an FPGA implementation on NRE, unit cost, performance, power and time to market, and recommend one.
outline: ASIC: high fixed NRE (masks, EDA, IP, packaging), low unit cost at volume, best speed and power
FPGA: near-zero NRE, higher unit cost, lower clock speed, more power, but reprogrammable in the field
Break-even volume analysis: difference in NRE divided by difference in unit cost
Schedule: an ASIC adds physical design, signoff and fabrication months; an FPGA can be re-programmed after a bug
Risk: respin cost of an ASIC versus bitstream update of an FPGA
Justified recommendation for 5,000 units and six months
answer: Use the cost figures of the ASIC chapter's worked example for the main chip: FPGA ₹1,800 per chip with no NRE; gate array ₹40 lakh NRE and ₹500 per chip; standard-cell ASIC ₹2 crore NRE and ₹250 per chip.

answer.text: Total chip cost for 5,000 boards (total = NRE + N × unit cost):
Break-even volumes against the FPGA:

answer: NRE: the FPGA needs none; an ASIC pays for masks, tools, IP licences, test programs and packaging up front. At 5,000 units the standard-cell ASIC is the most expensive option by far, because 5,000 is well below its break-even of 12,903.
Unit cost: the ASIC wins per chip (₹250 against ₹1,800), but that saving only pays back its NRE above the break-even volume.

Performance and power: an ASIC built from fixed gates and wires runs at a higher clock and uses less power and area for the same function; an FPGA pays for its programmable LUTs and switches. For a signal-processing board, check that the FPGA's DSP slices meet the sample rate; if they do, performance does not decide the case.

Time to market: an FPGA design can be on a board in weeks. A standard-cell ASIC needs synthesis, DFT, physical design and signoff, then several weeks of fabrication, packaging and test; even a gate array, with only metal masks, needs weeks of foundry time. Six months leaves no room for a respin.
Risk: an ASIC bug found after tapeout needs new masks, months and a second NRE. An FPGA bug is fixed with a new bitstream, even on boards already shipped.

Evaluation: the gate array is ₹25 lakh cheaper than the FPGA on paper, but that saving is lost with one respin (another ₹40 lakh) and its schedule leaves almost no margin in six months. The standard-cell ASIC is ruled out by both cost and time.

Recommendation: build the board on an FPGA. Ship on time, fix bugs in the field, and revisit a gate array or ASIC only if orders rise past the break-even volumes (about 3,100 for a gate array, 12,900 for a standard cell) and the design is stable.

bank.q: Discuss test cost metrics and test economics. Analyse the trade-off between external ATE testing, scan-based ATPG and BIST for a large logic chip.
outline: Cost drivers: tester time per device, pattern count, tester pin count and capital cost, yield learning
Test time equals pattern count times shift and capture cycles; more coverage usually means more patterns
ATE with scan ATPG: high coverage, needs a tester, more pins and memory for patterns
BIST: on-chip generation, runs at speed, but area overhead and limited diagnosis
Fault coverage versus defect level; escape cost and customer returns
Balanced scheme: BIST for memories and embedded blocks, scan ATPG for random logic
answer: Test cost per chip = test time × tester rate, plus the share of DFT area on every die, plus the cost of the chips that escape. Test economics balances these three.

Metrics: fault coverage (detected ÷ modelled faults), pattern count, test time per chip, test pins, tester memory for the patterns, DFT area overhead, and the defect level (bad chips shipped, in parts per million).

answer.text: Test time comes from scan shifting. For 1,000 patterns at a 50 MHz scan clock (20 ns) and a ₹3 per second tester:

answer: On 10 lakh chips that is ₹3,00,360 against ₹30,090. Ten chains need 20 scan pins, so pins are traded for time; on-chip test compression gets the same cut with fewer pins.

answer.text: Escapes: with yield Y and fault coverage T, the defect level is DL = 1 − Y<sup>(1 − T)</sup> (the Williams-Brown estimate). For Y = 90 %:

answer: So the last per cent of coverage cuts escapes ten times. For a car or a phone maker that returns a bad chip at many times its price, the extra patterns pay for themselves.

External ATE with functional patterns: no DFT area, but long hand-written test programs, low coverage of deep logic and an expensive tester that must run at full chip speed. It does not scale to large logic chips.

Scan-based ATPG on ATE: scan flip-flops cost a few per cent of area and some speed (the scan multiplexer), but ATPG reaches very high stuck-at and transition coverage automatically and pinpoints the failing flip-flop for diagnosis. The cost is tester time and pattern memory, as the table shows.

BIST: an LFSR and a MISR on the chip test at full speed with almost no tester time and only a few pins, and the same test can run in the field. But pseudo-random patterns miss hard-to-reach faults, the signature hides which bit failed, and the logic adds area. It suits regular blocks such as memories, where March tests cover the usual memory fault models.

Analysis: for random logic scan ATPG gives the best coverage per rupee; for memories BIST wins; boundary scan covers the board connections; functional tests remain only for speed binning and analog checks.
Recommended scheme: scan with compression and ATPG for the logic, memory BIST for every SRAM, boundary scan at the pins, and a coverage target set from the defect level the customer accepts.

bank.q: Compare full-custom and semi-custom design styles. When is each justified, and how does the choice change the design flow?
outline: Full-custom: every transistor drawn by hand, best area, speed and power, longest schedule and highest effort
Semi-custom: standard cells or gate arrays, library-based synthesis and place-and-route
Flow differences: full-custom needs schematic entry, layout editing, extraction and intensive DRC/LVS iteration
Semi-custom relies on characterised libraries, timing-driven synthesis and signoff with standard reports
Suitable cases: full-custom for high-volume processors, memories and analog; semi-custom for most digital logic
Cost, risk and reuse argument in the conclusion
answer: Full-custom: the designer sizes and draws every transistor and wire. Semi-custom: the designer works with pre-designed pieces, either library standard cells placed by tools (every mask still custom) or a masked gate array whose base transistors are already made (only metal masks custom).

answer.text: Comparison:

head: Point
Full-custom
Standard cell
Gate array
rows: Every mask; cells from a library
Contact, via and metal masks only
Lowest of the three (fixed transistor sizes, unused gates)
Medium; tools do placement and routing
Unit cost in the worked example

answer: How the flow changes in full-custom: schematic entry and transistor-level simulation (SPICE) replace synthesis; the layout is drawn in a layout editor, then extracted, and DRC, LVS and post-layout simulation are repeated by hand until clean. Timing comes from circuit simulation, not from a cell library.

How the flow changes in semi-custom: RTL is synthesised onto a characterised library; placement, clock-tree synthesis and routing are automatic; static timing analysis uses the library's delay tables; signoff runs standard DRC, LVS and timing reports. A gate array shortens the back end further because only the wiring is made.

answer.text: Cost against volume with the worked-example figures:
answer.pre:
gate array ↔ standard cell:   (₹2 crore − ₹40 lakh) ÷ (500 − 250) = 64,000 chips
standard cell ↔ full custom:  (₹8 crore − ₹2 crore) ÷ (250 − 200) = 12 lakh chips

answer: When full-custom is justified: very high volume (above about 12 lakh chips here), a block repeated millions of times (an SRAM bit cell, a standard cell itself), analog and RF circuits, and the critical datapaths of high-speed processors where a few per cent of speed or power sells the product.

When semi-custom is justified: almost all other digital logic. Standard cells give near-custom quality with a fraction of the effort and are the default for SoCs; gate arrays fit lower volumes, from about 3,100 chips (against an FPGA) to 64,000 (against standard cells) in the example, or when the design must reach silicon fast.

Risk and reuse: full-custom layouts must be redrawn for each process and each bug costs more effort; standard-cell RTL moves to a new process by re-synthesis, and libraries and IP are reused across projects.
Evaluation: the two styles are combined in practice. A modern SoC is a standard-cell chip that contains full-custom macros (SRAMs, PLLs, I/O cells), so each style is used where it pays.

Closing check: at 20 lakh chips, full custom costs ₹8 crore + 20 lakh × ₹200 = ₹48 crore and standard cell ₹2 crore + 20 lakh × ₹250 = ₹52 crore, so full custom wins only well above its 12-lakh break-even, and only if its longer schedule is acceptable.

bank.q: Analyse how floorplanning decisions propagate through placement and routing. Show what fails at signoff when a floorplan is poor.
outline: Macro positions and aspect ratio fix the distance between communicating blocks and the routing channels
Pin assignment sets where signals enter; the wrong side forces long detours
Utilisation too high leaves no space for the router: congestion and detours
Congestion raises wire length, which raises delay, dynamic power and crosstalk
Clock tree and power grid need space in the floorplan; ignoring them causes IR drop and skew failures
Feedback loop: congestion or timing violations force re-floorplanning
answer: The floorplan fixes the frame that placement and routing must work inside: core size, aspect ratio, macro positions, pin positions and the power grid. Later stages can move cells within that frame but cannot repair the frame itself.

answer.text: Start from the floorplan of the floorplanning chapter: a 3.0 mm × 3.0 mm core with hard blocks of 2.0, 1.5, 1.0 and 0.5 mm² and 1.8 mm² of standard cells:
answer.pre:
A<sub>core</sub> = 3.0 × 3.0 = 9.0 mm²
A<sub>used</sub> = 5.0 + 1.8 = 6.8 mm²     U = 6.8 ÷ 9.0 = 75.6 %
whitespace = 2.2 mm²; with 20 % routing margin 8.16 mm² ≤ 9.0 mm², 0.84 mm² spare

answer.text: Now squeeze the core to 2.7 mm × 2.7 mm to save area and follow the effects:
answer.pre:
A<sub>core</sub> = 7.29 mm²     U = 6.8 ÷ 7.29 = 93.3 %
needed with 20 % margin: 8.16 mm² > 7.29 mm², short by 0.87 mm²

answer: Placement: at 93 % there are no free sites near the macros, so cells that talk to each other are spread apart and the HPWL rises; buffers needed for long nets have nowhere to go.
Routing: demand for tracks exceeds supply in the channels between the macros. The router detours nets, adds vias and leaves some nets unrouted or with shorts, which shows up as DRC errors.
Timing: detoured wires are longer, so their resistance and capacitance rise and the critical paths miss the clock period (setup violations); hold fixing needs buffers that cannot be placed.
Power and noise: longer wires mean more switched capacitance and dynamic power; wires packed side by side couple more, so crosstalk glitches and delay changes appear.

Macro and pin decisions propagate the same way. A memory placed in the far corner from the processor that reads it makes every read path cross the die. Pins on the wrong side force every net to cross the core. A macro with its pins facing the die edge leaves no room to reach them.

Clock and power: a floorplan with no space for clock buffers gives large skew; straps that are too narrow, or blocks placed far from the supply pads, give IR drop that slows every gate in that region and can fail the IR-drop signoff check.

answer.text: What fails at signoff, and the floorplan cause:

head: Signoff check that fails
Floorplan cause
rows: DRC: shorts, spacing, opens from unrouted nets
Utilization too high; narrow channels between macros
Long detours; communicating blocks placed far apart
No room for clock and hold buffers
Power grid too thin; blocks far from the supply pads

answer: Feedback: these failures cannot be fixed by the router alone, so the team returns to the floorplan, moves macros, adds channels or enlarges the core, and runs placement and routing again. Each loop costs days, which is why floorplanning is checked early with congestion and IR-drop estimates.

Closing check: the 3.0 mm core keeps 0.84 mm² spare after the 20 % routing margin; the 2.7 mm core is 0.87 mm² short. Saving 1.71 mm² of area (9.0 − 7.29) costs a failed signoff, so the larger core is the right floorplan.

glossary.def: A chip manufactured for one fixed function, customised through masks at fabrication.
Register-transfer level: a description of sequential logic as registers and the combinational logic between them.
A list of cells and the nets that connect their pins, the usual output of synthesis.
A Verilog module, with no ports, that generates stimulus and checks the outputs of a design instance.
Design Under Test: the instantiated module that a test bench exercises.
Design for testability: on-chip structures added to make internal nodes controllable and observable from the pins.
Automatic test pattern generation: software that computes input patterns to detect modelled faults.
Built-in self-test: on-chip circuitry that generates test patterns and compresses the responses.
A series of scan flip-flops linked into a shift register so test data can be loaded and unloaded serially.
An abstract representation of a physical defect, such as a line stuck-at 0, used for test generation.
The final set of checks (timing, power, physical verification) that must pass before tapeout.
A style where the designer draws and optimises every transistor and its layout by hand.
A style that uses pre-characterised cells or a pre-built array and customises mainly the interconnection.
Lookup table: a small memory in an FPGA that holds the truth table of a combinational function.
Configurable logic block: an FPGA tile holding lookup tables, flip-flops and carry logic.
Field-programmable gate array: a chip whose logic cells and wiring are configured by a bitstream after manufacture.
Complex programmable logic device: a small programmable part with macrocells and a central switch matrix.
A pre-designed, verified functional block that is licensed and reused in a larger chip.
IP delivered as synthesizable HDL source, mapped to the user's technology at build time.
IP delivered as a fixed physical layout for one process, with guaranteed timing and area.
A processor supplied as HDL and implemented in the programmable or standard-cell fabric.
Logic placed around a reused block to adapt its signal names, bus protocol, clocks and resets to the surrounding system.
A connection between logic on two unrelated clocks, needing synchronisers or asynchronous FIFOs.
Assigning die area, macro positions, pin locations and power structure before placement.
Choosing the exact die coordinate of each cell with the aim of short wires and low congestion.
Creating the metal wires and vias that realise the nets between placed cells.
A pre-designed, characterised library gate of fixed height and variable width, placed in rows by tools.
An ASIC built on a pre-made base wafer of transistors, customised only by its metal and via masks.
Non-recurring engineering cost: the one-time cost of design, tools, masks and test programs.
The handoff of the final layout database (GDSII) to the foundry for mask making.
